topic: why satellites don't actually float -- they're in constant freefall (Newton's cannonball)
title: The 1687 Thought Experiment That Explains Why Satellites Never Fall
description: AI-narrated commentary: satellites aren't floating -- they're in constant freefall, a mechanism Isaac Newton described over 300 years before the first satellite ever launched. Why does the ISS never actually hit the ground? #space #science #shorts

hook_candidates.text: Newton once imagined a cannonball fired so fast it would never land.
Satellites don't float in orbit -- they're falling, nonstop, and always have been.
The ISS has been falling toward Earth for 28 years straight -- and never once hit the ground.
If gravity still works in space, why doesn't the ISS ever fall out of the sky?

payoff_mechanism: A satellite stays up because it moves sideways fast enough that Earth's surface curves away beneath it just as fast as it falls, so it keeps falling toward the ground without ever actually hitting it -- the exact idea behind Newton's cannonball.

beats.text: Newton imagined a cannonball that **never** lands.
Fire it fast enough and Earth **curves** away as fast as it falls.
That's literally how the ISS stays up -- **falling** for **28 years**, just too fast to hit the ground.
Still Newton's cannonball. Follow for more physics that flips your intuition.
